series.definition: USGS Minerals Yearbook world production. Exact commodity, form, form detail, units and unit detail identify this series. Latest publication vintage per source year and country, as identified in every row; source editions are not averaged. Minerals Yearbook world production CSV. Exact material/form/unit dimensions remain separate. Each country/source-year uses its latest available publication vintage; all publisher vintages remain in the downloadable original CSV archive.
limitations: Retained source edition acquired 1 November 2026; publisher coverage and revisions vary by country and year.
Missing or ineligible source cells remain unavailable. No interpolation, carry-forward, zero filling, numerical unit conversion or averaging is performed.
Country, territory and aggregate accounts remain separate. Historical geographies are not reassigned to current successor states.
Compare the exact source definition, physical basis, unit and year. A production index, a percentage, a physical quantity and an accounting estimate answer different questions.

Latest publication vintage per source year is a declared selection across Minerals Yearbook source tables, not a single frozen survey vintage. Table definitions and rounding may change; original table notes accompany every selected row.
Multiple rows in the same latest publication vintage are unavailable for mapping; their source rows remain attached. Missing latest-vintage values are never replaced by older numerical observations.
World/region totals, historical geographies and unresolved country labels remain in the all-vintages source archive and geography register; no boundary reassignment or worldwide sum is constructed.
Even an unchanged country label may span boundary or reporting changes, such as Sudan. A constant modern polygon does not establish comparable historical territory.
Production is separate from reserves, capacity, consumption or physical shipment flows. Material content and gross mass are separate native dimensions.

source_record.TABLE_NOTES: [1] Table includes data available through September 17, 2019. All data are reported unless otherwise noted. Grand totals and estimated data are rounded to no more than three significant digits; may not add to totals shown. [2] Primary nickel refers to a nickel product ready for use by downstream consuming industries and includes nickel chemicals and salts, ferronickel, nickel metal in various forms, nickel oxide sinter, and nickel pig iron. The U.S. Geological Survey does not use the terms Class I and Class II nickel as defined by the International Nickel Study Group (INSG). However, nickel metal reported here is generally equivalent to Class I nickel which is defined by INSG as nickel with a minimum nickel content of 99% in the form of briquets, cathodes (that is, electrolytic nickel), flakes or powders, granules, pellets, and rondelles. Ferronickel, nickel oxide sinter, and nickel pig iron are classified by INSG as Class II. Chemicals, although typically produced at refineries, are differentiated from production of metal when feasible.

source_record.TABLE_NOTES: [1] Table includes data available through March 24, 2021. All data are reported unless otherwise noted. Grand totals and estimated data are rounded to no more than three significant digits; may not add to totals shown. [2] Primary nickel refers to a nickel product ready for use by downstream consuming industries such as nickel chemicals and salts, ferronickel, nickel metal in various forms, nickel oxide sinter, and nickel pig iron (a form of ferronickel with nickel content typically less than 15%). The USGS does not use the terms Class I and Class II nickel as defined by the International Nickel Study Group (INSG). However, nickel metal reported here is generally equivalent to Class I nickel which is defined by INSG as nickel with a minimum nickel content of 99% in the form of briquets, cathodes (that is, electrolytic nickel), flakes or powders, granules, pellets, and rondelles. Ferronickel, nickel oxide sinter, and nickel pig iron are classified by INSG as Class II. Chemicals, although typically produced at refineries, are differentiated from production of metal when feasible. Several countries produced nickel-containing matte and other intermediates, but output of nickel in such materials has been excluded from this table to avoid double counting. Countries that produced intermediate products for export are listed in table 11.
